title: Boston Consulting Group eyes nation-building via better SL businesses | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 9 October 2026 00:00
-     - 19

By Nisthar Cassim

Encouraged by the resilience and rebound, as well as the growing acceptance of its expertise, global giant Boston Consulting Group (BCG) is keen to help businesses grow, thereby contributing to nation-building in Sri Lanka.

This vision was shared by BCG Asia Pacific Chairman Yasushi Sasaki and India Head, Managing Director and Senior Partner Rahul Jain, who are in Sri Lanka along with around 600 Managing Directors and Partners for their annual planning conference over three days.

“We find companies in Sri Lanka to be quite visionary, and they have the mindset to think bolder, take on transformations,” the BCG duo told the Daily FT in an interview. 

They said that BCG is seeing much greater client acceptance and, hence, want to help Sri Lankan businesses and the country.

“In the last 18 months, things have really shot up. We are looking at greater local presence. We have taken a small office space also and we want some of our people to be housed here. We want to grow our business and contribute to the growth of the nation and to the betterment of humanity,” Sasaki and Jain said.

“Business is only one piece. The other is always how much we can help in nation-building, in industry-building, and help the society at large,” emphasised Sasaki, who is in Sri Lanka for the first time.

Noting that there is strong demand in Sri Lanka, the BCG duo said the company’s role is to support these clients. 

“Firstly, we are keen to strengthen their business that will contribute to the society in Sri Lanka, and then one day, if they can move up their way to globalise the operation, that will be a great contribution to the global society. This is BCG’s mindset. We are really committed to Sri Lanka and to the success of our clients,” Sasaki and Jain added.

Regarded as a global consulting firm that partners with leaders in business and society to deliver transformative impact, BCG has over 2,300 experts globally of which over 600 are in the Asia Pacific. 

“We work with governments everywhere, as long as it is really value adding and constructive, and it helps in the right cause. To really make a deep impact in the functioning of the government, one needs to know the country really well. So we are in the working stages of that, and we do believe that in time to come, we will play a big role there as well,” the BCG duo added.

They also said that post-crisis, Sri Lanka has recovered commendably and has great potential for the future. “It [Sri Lanka] is promising in my view. After the crisis, Sri Lanka is back. That is a key work theme for BCG this week,” Sasaki said, adding that he looks forward to discussion with Sri Lankan CEOs.

“Sri Lanka has shown remarkable resilience and businesses learn resilience through the experience of crisis. That would be a great asset to guide the economy and business in the future amidst external uncertainties,” he added.

According to BCG, some of the current and emerging challenges for businesses and nations alike include Artificial Intelligence (AI) and geopolitics.

It was pointed out that global CEOs now understand the importance of AI as a necessity. They put AI as their topmost priority and are keen to master it to guide organisations effectively. Geopolitics, the BCG duo identified as a never-ending story.

“Great leaders are really good at training the geopolitical muscle itself. They try to be resilient and adaptive to the situation. If you can overcome these challenges, there are great opportunities for countries and businesses,” they emphasised.

The BCG duo also stressed that Sri Lanka must better harness the India opportunity, being the geographically strategic neighbour. 

“We are seeing growing interest to explore opportunities in the Indian. Certainly, there are a lot of collaboration opportunities, and it can be a win-win. We don’t need to compete with each other but collaborate,” pointed out Jain. “There is enough opportunity from a supply chain point of view, synergistic point of view to support each other. Businesses from both countries must leverage each other as a market, but also as a supply source for both products and services,” he added.

Sasaki stressed the importance of Sri Lanka retaining its great young talent within the country. “There is a role for the Government as well as business leaders, because talent will determine the future of the country,” he said. 

BCG sees banking and finance in Sri Lanka among growth sectors. “It is the foundation for the economy. The sector should look at attracting more capital from outside the country, and then hopefully, as a next step, be aspirational to expand the business outside Sri Lanka,” the BCG duo said, adding that leveraging AI was key as well.

BCG also listed agriculture and tourism as natural strengths for Sri Lanka, and said they must be leveraged better with innovation and productivity. Logistics is another growth opportunity given Sri Lanka’s strategic location and aspiration to be a regional hub, for which improved efficiency is required. BCG also believes textile and apparel to be among sectors in which Sri Lanka can expand drawing lessons from Vietnam and Bangladesh.  

“Sri Lanka has some great apparel companies who can play a much bigger role in the global supply chain,” the BCG duo added.

They also emphasised the importance of developing small and medium enterprises/entrepreneurs (SMEs). “Our message is, without SMEs, no nation grows. Holistic development in a country requires the uplifting of SMEs. Whether it is financing them or giving them market opportunities, governments need to think of how to uplift SMEs because without that, the nation doesn’t work,” they stressed, adding that “if SMEs are aspirational, BCG is willing to help.”

title: Scrutiny intensifies on NDB Board and auditors over Rs. 13.6 b fraud | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 9 October 2026 00:21
-     - 31

Scrutiny of National Development Bank’s (NDB) Board and external auditors intensified as Parliament’s Committee on Public Finance (CoPF) questioned why no Board member or senior official or auditor had been held responsible for the Rs. 13.6 billion fraud at the bank. The audit regulator’s findings on the auditors are due within two weeks.

CoPF Chair Dr. Harsha de Silva said the forensic review by Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu India LLP did not include any member of senior management in its list of those involved.

“So no senior person has been found fault with. Some senior person has to finally take responsibility for the integrity of the numbers presented to the auditor,” Dr. de Silva said. He added that if the external auditor had done its job properly, the blame could not rest only with junior officers.

“Are any heads going to roll? Is anyone going to be responsible for this at the end of the day? Are there conflicts of interest here, involving the external auditors and audit committees?” he asked.

Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe told the Committee that the failure ran through every layer of the bank’s oversight. Internal auditors, the Chief Financial Officer (CFO), the Board Audit Committee, and the Board itself had all failed to detect the fraud, even after seeing and signing the financial statements.

“That tells us something has gone wrong in the internal control mechanism,” he said. “With a lot of respect to the accounting profession, none of these experts, the CFOs, audit committees, and the best accountants in this country, were able to detect this when it was presented on their table and they signed off.”

CBSL Deputy Governor K.G.P. Sirikumara said the forensic review had also examined how NDB’s Board-level and management risk committees performed.

“As much as the Sri Lanka Accounting and Auditing Standards Monitoring Board (SLAASMB) looked at the external auditor’s role, the mandate of the forensic auditor is to look at the processes and governance requirements as well. In that aspect, they have looked into several risk-related committees, the Operational Risk Management Committee, the Business Operations Risk Sounding Board, the Business Assurance Office, and so on. They looked at whether these have performed their role properly and whether the proper, adequate, and required coordination has been there,” Sirikumara said.

“Based on those findings, when we look at the bank’s management from the bank supervisor’s point of view, certain people may be found responsible for governance defaults or even negligence,” he added.

Sirikumara said the forensic auditor had not attributed responsibility for the fraudulent transactions themselves to those in oversight roles. Even so, anyone found responsible for governance or internal control failures would face consequences from the CBSL as the bank’s regulator, though these need not be criminal. The individuals already identified had committed financial crimes, not mere negligence, he said. Where negligence is found, whether it amounts to criminal negligence would depend on the circumstances.

The Governor said any key management personnel found negligent or wilfully involved in the fraud would fail the CBSL’s fit and proper assessment. “Obviously, I think that should be the end of this person’s suitability to serve any financial institution,” he said.

The SLAASMB told the CoPF that it has completed a separate investigation into whether NDB’s external auditors carried out their work in line with auditing standards. The report, prepared by the SLAASMB’s technical team, was presented to its Board last Friday and will be released within two weeks. Under its mandate, it will be shared with the CBSL and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

Dr. de Silva pressed the SLAASMB to look beyond the NDB case at the conduct and structure of the audit industry. He questioned whether auditors were honestly examining company records, or whether those signing off were doing so blindly or negligently.

“What about market capture? There are three or four audit firms, at least the big ones, that share a fair chunk of the market. Are there conflicts of interest? Where are they placed? What roles do they play? How politically important are they? Would you go into all of that?” he asked.

The Committee was told the issue merited a dedicated session with the SLAASMB Board. The SLAASMB was set up under an Act passed in 1995 and carries a wide mandate, but works with limited resources. Dr. de Silva agreed to hold a separate hearing with the SLAASMB Board, saying it was in the interest of financial system stability. The CoPF also asked the SLAASMB to share whatever it could from its NDB report once it is finalised.

MP Ravi Karunanayake said NDB’s CEFT receivables had quadrupled in a year to more than Rs. 12 billion in 2025, a figure disclosed in financial statements the external auditor certified as true and fair without raising concerns. CEFT, the Common Electronic Fund Transfer switch operated by LankaPay, is the national instant interbank transfer system. He asked who in the bank signed off on responses to audit queries about the balance.

CBSL officials said NDB’s accounts are signed by the CFO, the Chief Executive Officer, and the Chairman on behalf of the Board. The Board Audit Committee vouches for the integrity of the statements and the auditor’s management letter before they reach the Board.

The Governor maintained that the fraud, confirmed by the forensic review to be confined to NDB, had no impact on financial system stability. “Even within the bank, not a single deposit has been compromised. There is no spillover effect of this transaction to the other banks,” he said.

Dr. de Silva said the CBSL’s three-page summary of Deloitte’s six key findings contained nothing new. The Governor said the CBSL was awaiting the Attorney General’s advice on sharing the full report, given a non-disclosure clause in NDB’s agreement with Deloitte India.

LankaPay officials told the CoPF that it will float a request for proposals (RFP) for a central fraud monitoring system, due by September 2027, with requirements drawn up by local banking specialists and overseas fraud experts. 

The Committee asked the Governor for a comprehensive note on the fraud’s causes and the CBSL’s preventive measures once it has studied the forensic review and the SLAASMB report.

title: Customs ends manual document submissions from 19 Oct. | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 9 October 2026 00:20
-     - 14

Sri Lanka Customs will stop accepting manual document submissions for Full Container Load (FCL) imports under office code CBHQ1 from 19 October, as it moves to a paperless Customs declaration system.

FCL refers to shipments in which a single importer’s goods fill an entire container. Customs said in a notice that paperless processing of Customs Declarations (CusDecs), the documents importers file to clear goods, was launched for FCL imports on 1 October.

All importers must obtain a digital signature and complete registration by 19 October to access the paperless service. Customs said about 2,000 importers had already obtained digital signatures, while a significant number were yet to complete registration.

Importers who have already registered must use the paperless system immediately and should not submit documents manually, even before the deadline, Customs said. The Department urged the remaining importers to register before 19 October to comply with the new system.
